statement: What is the least positive integer $n$ such that every set of $n$ distinct integers chosen from $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 30\}$ contains two numbers that differ by exactly $4$?

choices.misconception: I used pigeonhole on the 4 remainders modulo 4, but two numbers with the same remainder need not differ by exactly 4, only by a multiple of 4.
I split 1 to 30 into eight blocks of four consecutive numbers, but two numbers in the same block differ by at most 3, never by 4.
I split the numbers into four chains by remainder mod 4 and took half of each chain rounded down, 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 14, then added 1, but a chain of 7 allows 4.
I found the largest set with no two numbers differing by 4, which has 16 elements, and gave that instead of one more than it.

hints: Which numbers can conflict with each other? Group them.
Only numbers with the same remainder modulo $4$ can differ by $4$. Each remainder class is a chain $r, r+4, r+8, \ldots$ in which neighbours conflict. Find the largest safe set, then add $1$.
The chains have lengths $8, 8, 7, 7$. From a chain of length $L$ you can take at most $\lceil L/2 \rceil$ numbers, and this is reached by taking every other one.

solutions.reliable: Split $\{1, \ldots, 30\}$ into four chains by remainder modulo $4$: $1, 5, \ldots, 29$ and $2, 6, \ldots, 30$ have $8$ terms each; $3, 7, \ldots, 27$ and $4, 8, \ldots, 28$ have $7$ terms each. Two numbers differ by exactly $4$ only when they are neighbours in the same chain. In a chain of length $L$ a set with no two neighbours has at most $\lceil L/2 \rceil$ elements (pair up consecutive terms; each pair holds at most one chosen number, plus one leftover if $L$ is odd), and taking the 1st, 3rd, 5th, ... terms achieves it. So the largest safe set has $4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16$ elements, for example $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 18, 19, 20, 25, 26, 27, 28\}$. Hence $16$ numbers are not enough, while any $17$ must put two neighbours of some chain together. The least $n$ is $17$. A computer search over safe sets confirms the maximum of $16$. The idea: the least number that forces a pattern is one more than the largest set that avoids it.
